name: Rabindranath Tagore
info: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) was a Bengali poet, songwriter, playwright, novelist and educator from Calcutta, the first Indian, and the first non-European, to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, who wrote the words of the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

facts.born: 7 May 1861 in the Jorasanko mansion, Calcutta; youngest of 13 surviving children of Debendranath Tagore and Sarada Devi, a Pirali Brahmin family at the forefront of the Bengal renaissance
facts.died: 7 August 1941, aged 80, in an upstairs room of the Jorasanko mansion where he was born, after five years of chronic pain and two long periods of illness
facts.role: Poet, author, playwright, composer, painter and social reformer; manager of the family estates at Shelaidaha (from 1890); founder of the school at Santiniketan (1901) and of Visva-Bharati (foundation stone 1918, inaugurated 1921); Nobel Prize in Literature (1913)
facts.known: Gitanjali; the novels Gora and Ghare-Baire; the short stories of Galpaguchchha; some 2,230 songs, known as Rabindrasangit; the words of India's "Jana Gana Mana" and Bangladesh's "Amar Sonar Bangla"; Visva-Bharati University; paintings taken up at sixty; the renunciation of his knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh

t: Born in 1861 into a Calcutta family at the centre of the Bengal renaissance, Tagore wrote his first poems as a child, managed the family estates in rural Bengal and drew on that life in his short stories, poems and songs.

He translated his Gitanjali into English in 1912 and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, the first Indian and first non-European to do so, then founded Visva-Bharati as a school and university meant to link India and the world.

A critic of nationalism who also denounced British rule, he renounced his knighthood after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919, and he disagreed with Gandhi on several matters, while some critics judged his English translations weak.
dyk: At sixteen Tagore published poems under the pseudonym Bhanusimha, claiming they were the lost works of a newly discovered 17th-century Vaishnava poet, and regional experts accepted them as such.
ev: Born in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the youngest of 13 surviving children
Presents poems as the lost works of a 17th-century poet, Bhanusimha, and debuts in the short story with "Bhikharini"
Begins managing the family estates at Shelaidaha and publishes the Manasi poems
Moves to Santiniketan to found an ashram with an experimental school
Learns in November that he has won the Nobel Prize in Literature
Renounces his knighthood after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
Visva-Bharati is inaugurated three years after its foundation stone was laid
Dies at Jorasanko on 7 August, aged 80

sections.early:
Rabindranath Tagore, nicknamed Rabi, was born on 7 May 1861 in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the youngest of 13 surviving children of Debendranath Tagore (1817–1905) and Sarada Devi (1830–1875). The name Tagore is an anglicised form of Thakur; the family were Pirali Brahmins, a group that historically carried a stigmatised connotation. His mother died in his early childhood and his father travelled widely, so servants raised him. The household was at the forefront of the Bengal renaissance, hosting literary magazines, theatre and recitals of Bengali and Western classical music, and Debendranath invited Dhrupad musicians to teach the children. His brothers included the philosopher and poet Dwijendranath, Satyendranath, the first Indian appointed to the Indian Civil Service, and the musician and playwright Jyotirindranath.

Tagore largely avoided classroom schooling and preferred to roam the manor or nearby Bolpur and Panihati. His brother Hemendranath tutored him and made him swim the Ganges, trek and wrestle, and he learned drawing, anatomy, geography, history, literature, mathematics, Sanskrit and English, his least favourite subject. His time at Presidency College lasted a single day. After his upanayan at eleven he toured India with his father from February 1873, visiting Santiniketan and Amritsar before reaching the hill station of Dalhousie, where he read biographies and studied history, astronomy, science and Sanskrit.
sections.rise:
By 1877 Tagore had completed a set of major works, among them a long poem in the Maithili style of Vidyapati. As a joke he claimed they were the lost works of a newly discovered 17th-century Vaishnava poet, Bhanusimha, and regional experts accepted them. That year he also debuted in the short-story genre with "Bhikharini", and the collections Sandhya Sangit (1882) and Prabhat Sangit (1883) followed. His father wanted him to become a barrister, so in 1878 he enrolled at a public school in Brighton, England, and briefly read law at University College London before leaving to study Shakespeare and Thomas Browne on his own. He returned to Bengal in 1880 without a degree.

In 1883 he married Mrinalini Devi, then nine years old, a common practice at the time; they had five children, two of whom died in childhood. The suicide in 1884 of Kadambari Devi, his brother Jyotirindranath's wife and a close friend, left him distraught for years. After his return his poems, stories and novels had a profound influence in Bengal but received little national attention. In 1890 he began managing the family estates at Shelaidaha, in present-day Bangladesh, where he published the Manasi poems and travelled the Padma River on the family barge.
sections.deeds:
The years 1891 to 1895, called his Sadhana period after one of his magazines, were his most productive. In them he wrote more than half the stories of the 84-story Galpaguchchha, among them "Kabuliwala" and "Kshudita Pashan", drawing on what he saw of poor villagers while managing the estates. He met Gagan Harkara, through whom he came to know the Baul Lalon Shah, whose folk songs influenced him and which he worked to popularise. In 1901 he moved to Santiniketan to found an ashram with a prayer hall, an experimental school, gardens and a library.

He translated his 1910 Gitanjali into English in 1912 and shared it in London with admirers including William Butler Yeats and Ezra Pound; in November 1913 he learned that he had won the Nobel Prize in Literature. The Swedish Academy appreciated the idealistic and, for Westerners, accessible character of a small body of his translated work centred on Gitanjali: Song Offerings. The foundation stone of Visva-Bharati was laid on 24 December 1918 and it was inaugurated three years later, with teaching often under trees; Tagore contributed his Nobel prize money and wrote the students' textbooks. In 1921, with the agricultural economist Leonard Elmhirst, he set up the Institute for Rural Reconstruction, later Shriniketan. His songs, about 2,230 in all, include "Jana Gana Mana", first sung in 1911 and adopted as India's national anthem in 1950, and "Amar Sonar Bangla", which became Bangladesh's in 1971. At sixty he took up painting, and his works were exhibited across Europe.
sections.opponents:
Tagore's politics drew anger from several sides. He opposed imperialism and denounced the British Raj, and evidence produced in the Hindu–German Conspiracy Trial and later accounts affirm his awareness of the Ghadarites and that he sought Japanese support, yet he also lampooned the Swadeshi movement and rebuked Gandhi's charkha cult in the 1925 essay The Cult of the Charkha. According to Amartya Sen, he rebelled against strongly nationalist forms of the independence movement while insisting on India's right to be independent. In his view British administration was a "political symptom of our social disease", and even for the very poor "there can be no question of blind revolution"; he preferred "steady and purposeful education". His essay "Nationalism in India" was scorned and praised. In late 1916 Indian expatriates plotted to assassinate him in a San Francisco hotel, and the plan failed when they fell into an argument.

He also criticised Gandhi directly. In 1934 he rebuked Gandhi for calling the Bihar earthquake divine retribution for the oppression of Dalits. After a warm first meeting with Mussolini in 1926 he felt compelled to denounce Fascism in The Manchester Guardian. His work met mixed judgements: Graham Greene doubted that anyone but Yeats could take his poems seriously, and Yeats himself wrote that Tagore had published "sentimental rubbish" and "wrecked his reputation". E. M. Forster found that The Home and the World had lost its charms in translation. His novels remain among the least appreciated of his works.
sections.last:
Dutta and Robinson describe his last years as those of a "peripatetic litterateur". Between 1878 and 1932 he had set foot in more than thirty countries on five continents. In 1932 he visited Persia and Iraq, and in 1933 Sri Lanka, in what was his final foreign tour. In Iraq a Bedouin chief quoted a saying of the Prophet to him, and Tagore wrote in his diary that he was "startled into recognising in his words the voice of essential humanity". His dislike of communalism and nationalism deepened. In 1937 his paintings were removed by the Nazi regime from a Berlin palace, and five were included in the inventory of "degenerate art" compiled in 1941–1942.

In these years fifteen new volumes appeared, among them the prose-poem works Punashcha (1932), Shes Saptak (1935) and Patraput (1936), and the dance-dramas Chandalika (1938) and Shyama (1939). His interest turned to science, as in the essays of Visva-Parichay (1937) and the stories of Se (1937) and Galpasalpa (1941). His last five years were marked by chronic pain and two long illnesses, which began when he lost consciousness in late 1937 and again in late 1940, from the second of which he never recovered. He died on 7 August 1941, aged 80, in an upstairs room of the Jorasanko mansion where he was raised. His last poem was dictated on 30 July to A. K. Sen, a day before a scheduled operation.
sections.legacy:
Tagore's compositions were chosen by two nations as national anthems, and Sri Lanka's anthem was inspired by his work; his song "Banglar Mati Banglar Jol" is the state anthem of West Bengal. Amartya Sen called him a "towering figure" and a "deeply relevant and many-sided contemporary thinker". His songs are central to Bengali life: the Modern Review observed that there was in Bengal "no cultured home where Rabindranath's songs are not sung or at least attempted to be sung". Eight museums commemorate him, three in India and five in Bangladesh, and Jorasanko Thakur Bari, his birthplace, is now part of the Rabindra Bharati University campus.

Abroad his reception varied. Through translations he influenced Pablo Neruda, Gabriela Mistral, Octavio Paz and Juan Ramón Jiménez, and in Japan the Nobel laureate Yasunari Kawabata. He co-founded Dartington Hall School. His lecture tours in the United States in 1916–1917 were widely attended, but controversies, possibly fictive, damaged his popularity and sales in Japan and North America after the late 1920s, concluding with his "near total eclipse" outside Bengal. William Radice asked what place his poems hold in world literature, and many readers hold that the translations never matched the Bengali originals. His Nobel Prize was stolen from the Visva-Bharati vault in March 2004, and the Swedish Academy presented two replicas that December.

summary: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941), born in Calcutta, wrote poems, stories, novels, plays and about 2,230 songs in Bengali, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 and founded Visva-Bharati. He wrote the words of the anthems of India and Bangladesh, criticised nationalism and British rule alike, and renounced his knighthood in 1919.

T. Dasgupta, Social Thought of Rabindranath Tagore: A Historical Analysis (Abhinav Publications, 1993)
K. Dutta, Rabindranath Tagore: The Myriad-Minded Man (Saint Martin's Press, 1995)
notes: Nobel: the lead says he was the first non-European to win a Nobel Prize in any category; the Poetry section says he was the second non-European to receive a Nobel Prize after Theodore Roosevelt. These contradict; the text follows the lead (first Indian and first non-European). The editor should check.

Early life: the article says Kadambari's suicide came in 1884 'soon after he married' (marriage 1883). Mrinalini's years are 1874–1902; the article says in the Santiniketan section that 'his wife and two of his children died' there (from 1901); her death year is left out of the text.
The Brighton paragraph says his nephew and niece were sent to live with him in 1877, a year before he went to England in 1878; left out as inconsistent. The Bhanusimha poems are dated 'by 1877'.
Santiniketan/Shantiniketan and Shelaidaha/Shilaidaha are spelt variously in the article; one spelling each used.

'Jana Gana Mana' is called the first of five stanzas of the Brahmo hymn Bharot Bhagyo Bidhata; the article says it was adopted in 1950 by the Constituent Assembly; first sung 1911 at the Calcutta session of Congress.
The politics section says Tagore was 'key in resolving a Gandhi–Ambedkar dispute' on separate electorates; left out as a claim stated without detail.

Left out: the Sikhism poems, Tagore's travels in detail (Latin America, Hungary, Southeast Asia, Soviet Union), the Greater India Society, the Guruvayoor temple campaign, the long list of Western translators and admirers, Hibbert Lectures, the in popular culture section, Radhakrishnan, the blue plaque and Edinburgh bust, and the Wikipedia's rankings ('the greatest poet India has produced').
The 'wrecked his reputation' quotation is Yeats's as the article gives it. The 'cult of the charkha' essay is the article's 'The Cult of the Charkha' (1925).
